title: Otis Cloud EMS 2.0
subtitle: Turning a legacy monitoring system into a proactive cloud platform — by designing for fear, not efficiency
summary: A legacy monitoring system made proactive

meta.label: Team
meta.value: 2 UI Designers · 10+ Engineers · 1 PM · 1 Project Manager

meta.label: Recognition
meta.value: 2026 Red Dot Award: Brands & Communication Design

value: Otis's clients manage complex properties worldwide, but legacy on-premise infrastructure made real-time monitoring nearly impossible. That opacity forced reactive maintenance — waiting for elevators to fail — driving up downtime, cost, and friction. The hypothesis: real-time health data and predictive alerts could cut emergency repair calls by 20%.

I was brought in as Lead Designer to move this rigid system to a cloud-native, globally scalable ecosystem. But the mandate arrived as a slogan — "move our legacy system to the cloud, and make it scale globally" — with no user, no scenario, no definition of success. "Cloud" is a technical action, not a user need.
So my first move wasn't visual. It was turning the slogan back into an answerable question.

items.label: Constraint 1
items.title: Bridging the technical gap
items.desc: Expert tools that don't overwhelm non-technical users.

items.label: Constraint 2
items.title: High-stakes compliance
items.desc: Usability inside strict safety and data rules.

items.label: Constraint 3
items.title: Global diversity
items.desc: One global system that respects local nuance.

indexedSections.title: Four moves from slogan to problem

blocks.title: Strip the solution back to the problem

value: When I aligned with the business and PM, the "requirement" was crisp: "We need a real-time monitoring dashboard." Classic solution-as-requirement. So instead of taking the order, I traced it back with a few whys: Why real-time monitoring? Clients can't see equipment health. Why does that matter? Because unseen, elevators only get fixed after they break — reactive maintenance: expensive, disruptive, a constant source of complaints.

items.label: The actual problem
items.desc: Clients are trapped in a reactive firefighting model — and can't move to proactive prevention.

blocks.value: That single reframe — from "build a dashboard" to "move clients from reactive firefighting to proactive prevention" — set the direction for everything after.

steps.label: Why?
steps.text: Clients can't see equipment health live.

steps.label: Why does that matter?
steps.text: They learn of failures only after a breakdown.

steps.label: Why is that bad?
steps.text: Every fix is reactive: expensive, disruptive, complaint-generating.

steps.label: The root problem
steps.text: Clients are stuck firefighting, never preventing.

blocks.title: Go to the field — every need I had was second-hand

value: Before committing, I hit the brakes on one realization: every "user need" I had was second-hand, relayed to HQ in New York through sales, support, and engineering — layers of distortion. The user described in a conference room and the one standing in a machine room could easily be two different people. I couldn't even follow the vocabulary — car call, hall call, group dispatch.

With no researcher and a lean team (me + 2 UI designers), a months-long study was off the table. So I took the lowest-cost path to the highest-fidelity truth: on-site contextual inquiry at high-traffic NYC properties, standing behind users as they worked.

blocks.label: Field visit — the front-desk workstation at One Columbus Circle, where the legacy system actually lives

value: The field flipped our assumptions. Everyone, myself included, had assumed users wanted efficiency. What I saw was non-technical building managers operating in fear.
One manager stuck with me. For a trivial operation he'd phone an Otis engineer rather than press the button himself. Why?

blocks.value: I'm afraid I'll shut down every elevator in the building.

That was the moment. We were designing for efficiency; users were stuck in fear. I named it consequence anxiety: the dread of an irreversible, catastrophic mistake. It made them offload even simple tasks to engineers — which meant our usage data was a false positive. The real pain point was invisible in the data, and only surfaced on-site.

blocks.label: The trap
blocks.value: Usage data looked healthy because engineers did the work managers feared to touch. The metric wasn't measuring adoption — it was measuring avoidance.

value: The hard part: fear doesn't fit in a PRD, and engineers can't sprint-plan an emotion. So my final discovery move was translating the feeling into testable requirements. I codified "users operate in fear" into a principle — psychological safety before efficiency — and broke it into three things engineering could build and validate:

items.title: Strong confirmation
items.desc: Irreversible, high-stakes actions need explicit confirmation.

items.title: Safe defaults
items.desc: The risky path is always deliberate, never accidental.

items.title: Plain-language labels
items.desc: Jargon like "car call" swapped for plain words — unlabeled call types caused guesswork in testing.

blocks.value: To hold the team to one axis, I defined two lean personas around the core tension:

items.label: Action
items.title: Field Engineer
items.desc: Technical, occasional user fixing issues on-site. Needs real-time status, dense data and low-friction flows.

items.label: Oversight
items.title: Building Manager
items.desc: Non-technical daily user running operations and tenants. Needs guidance, plain labels and confirmation before committing.

blocks.label: The alignment
blocks.value: For the first time the business goals — cloud, adoption, cost reduction — and the user goal — don't let me make a catastrophic mistake — shared one definition of success.

indexedSections.title: From insight to a shippable system

blocks.value: With the problem framed, execution followed a phased, de-risked path: discovery and quick wins first — low-risk UX improvements to build stakeholder confidence — then validation and workflow cleanup, then beta and a longer-term AI vision.

items.title: Dashboard & AI Copilot
items.desc: A centralized dashboard for real-time service visibility, paired with the "Ask Otis" AI Copilot to surface insights and guide next steps while keeping users in control.

items.title: Traffic Control & Monitoring
items.desc: Modular tools letting security teams and engineers manage calls, secure floors, and schedule operations in real time.

items.title: Health & Energy
items.desc: AI-powered insights monitor elevator health and energy use to surface early risks, predict maintenance, and cut consumption.

items.title: New User Guide
items.desc: Guided onboarding with contextual tutorials that shorten training time and build confidence faster.

indexedSections.title: Scaling "safe and legible" beyond my own screens

blocks.value: With my two UI designers I extended the design system with the pieces the old platform never had — a full charting library and a plain-spoken empty-state and iconography set — so "safe and legible" scaled beyond the screens I touched, and every new surface inherited the same guardrails.

indexedSections.title: From dreaded chore to daily tool

value: Cloud EMS 2.0 launched in early September, modernizing elevator management across 10+ core workflows and three user roles, and automating complex edge cases.

Beyond the numbers, the shift was behavioral: building managers began operating the system themselves instead of defaulting to Otis engineers. The platform went from a dreaded chore to a high-velocity tool — and became the mandate for my next initiative: reimagining enterprise security controls.
